document.title: National Security Directive 3. Subject: U.S. Policy Toward Afghanistan, February 13, 1989
document.authors: White House (Bush administration, National Security Council)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Soviet Withdrawal from Afghanistan 1989 | National Security Archive
document.note: Issued two days before the last Soviet soldier left, the heavily redacted directive reaffirms Reagan policy of supporting the resistance and 'working in concert with Pakistan'. It shows the US expected Najibullah's imminent fall, rejected Soviet proposals limiting US options on aid, and would treat Soviet bombing after Feb 15 as a Geneva violation.

organizations.name: Soviet Union
organizations.notes: Withdrew forces from Afghanistan; backed the Soviet-imposed Afghan government. The directive warns against bombing after 15 February 1989.

organizations.name: Resistance
organizations.notes: Recipient of U.S. assistance. The directive stresses promoting Resistance cohesion and avoiding support for any single faction.

organizations.name: Pakistan
organizations.notes: The U.S. works in concert with Pakistan to promote Resistance cohesion and a peaceful political succession.

organizations.name: Soviet-imposed government of Afghanistan
organizations.notes: The directive refers to its expected fall.

organizations.name: AID
organizations.notes: Oversees humanitarian programs in cooperation with Pakistan and the Resistance.

organizations.name: United Nations
organizations.notes: Runs a humanitarian effort to bring food into Afghanistan; the U.S. supports it if nationwide and with Resistance cooperation or acquiescence.

organizations.name: Director of Central Intelligence
organizations.notes: Coordinates with the Secretary of State on informing Congress.

organizations.name: National Security Council
organizations.notes: The directive was issued by the White House; NSC review declassified it in part in 2008.

places.name: Afghanistan
places.significance: Subject of the policy; the Soviet withdrawal and succession arrangements take place there.

places.name: Pakistan
places.significance: Partner of the U.S. in supporting the Resistance; hosts Afghan refugees.

events.description: President Bush issues National Security Directive 3 on U.S. policy toward Afghanistan after the Soviet withdrawal.
Deadline after which Soviet bombing of Afghan targets would be regarded as a serious violation of the Geneva Accords.
Soviet forces complete their withdrawal from Afghanistan (described as marking the victory of the Afghan struggle).
President Bush issues National Security Directive 3 on US policy toward Afghanistan after Soviet withdrawal.
Withdrawal of Soviet forces from Afghanistan, ending a decade-long struggle.
Deadline after which Soviet bombing of Afghan targets would be regarded by US as a serious violation of the Geneva Accords.

relationships.detail: The U.S. policy was to assist the Afghan struggle with Pakistan and others, and it will work in concert with Pakistan.
relationships.quote: Working in concert with Pakistan, the United States should use its influence and resources to (1) promote Resistance cohesion

relationships.detail: The U.S. assists the Resistance and promotes its cohesion, though it favors no single faction.
relationships.quote: promote a peaceful political succession, rather than support any individual or faction

relationships.detail: Pakistan cooperates with the U.S. on humanitarian programs and assistance for the Resistance.
relationships.quote: Humanitarian programs overseen by AID or other U. S. government agencies in cooperation with Pakistan and the Resistance should continue.

relationships.detail: The Afghan government is described as imposed by the Soviets.
relationships.quote: prior to the fall of the Soviet imposed government of Afghanistan

relationships.detail: The U.S. is prepared to engage in discussions on Soviet initiatives but will limit no options before the fall of the Kabul government.
relationships.quote: the United States should be prepared to engage in discussions but should take no action limiting U. S. options

relationships.detail: US policy was to assist, with Pakistan and others, the Afghan struggle against Soviet occupation; directive orders working in concert with Pakistan.
relationships.quote: U. S. policy throughout has been to assist, with Pakistan and others, in the achievement of that objective

key_claims: U.S. policy aimed to promote Resistance cohesion and a peaceful political succession without backing any individual or faction.
The U.S. sought to prevent a new Afghan government that was pro-Soviet, pro-Iranian or messianic-Islamic.
The U.S. would treat Soviet bombing in Afghanistan after 15 February 1989 as a serious violation of the Geneva Accords.
The U.S. would keep options open and not limit assistance to the Resistance before the fall of the Soviet-imposed government.
The U.S. would assure the USSR it wanted a neutral, non-aligned Afghan government not hostile to the Soviets.
The U.S. would continue humanitarian programs with Pakistan and the Resistance and support nationwide UN food aid.
